It is most interesting to browse through the Annals of Psi Upsilon and discover how
our various Chapters came into being. Once past the initial expansion of Psi Upsilon,
it seems that every prospective Chapter untU recent days had to make its way along
an arduous and lengthy path before receiving eventual approval from existing Chapters
assembled in Convention.
Having read through the history of the respective Chapters, I have come to the
conclusion that those which submitted their humble petitions year after year had to be
imbued with something more than just the desire to become a part of Psi UpsUon. First,
the founding groups had to be selective. They could not petition several fraternities
SimuUaneously. They had to detemaine that Psi UpsUon was the fraternity they wanted
and then pursue that goal by the petition route. This demand that they make a choice
before petitioning had a pronounced effect on the Chapters which were accepted into
the circle of our Fraternity. They already were obsessed with the meaning of member
ship in Psi UpsUon.
But, as I see it, there was a whole lot more that was required of those who sought
admission into the sacred rites of Psi Upsilon. After choosing to seek affiliation with
our Fraternity, the next step required courage, determination and dedication. These are
admirable traits in any one person. They are even more admirable when a group of
young men is able to summon up coUectively the virtues which encompass courage,
determination and dedication. In joining together to set out on the long, difficuU road
to Psi Upsilon brotherhood, each individual had to contribute his share of this courage,
determination and dedication.
Probably one of the most prolonged struggles by a group of undergraduates was that
waged by the petitioners for the Rho Chapter at the University of Wisconsin. Inspired
by a nucleus of Psi UpsUon alumni who lived in and about Madison in 1851, the first
petition was presented a year later at the Convention held with the Psi Chapter.
Petition after petition foUowed the original presentation, extending for an incredible
thuty-eight years. It was not untU the Convention of 1896 that approval was won by a
succession of young Wisconsin undergraduates, petitioners who had never countenanced
abandoning their ultimate goal.
The history of the founding of the Rho Chapter at the University of Wisconsin is
compelling reading for any member of our Fratemity. The principal detractors of Psi
Upsilon's appearance on the Madison campus were the other fratemities aUeady
established there. With consistent regularity these opponents let it be known, among
those attending the Psi UpsUon Conventions each year, that Rho Kappa UpsUon, the
local formed for the purpose of petitioning our Fraternity, was unworthy of considera
tion by an organization with the prestige of Psi Upsilon.
Surely there is no counterpart to the Rho Kappa UpsUon's courage, determination and
dedication anywhere in the chronicles of Greek Letter Societies. Undergraduate
generation after undergraduate generation displayed more than ordinary courage,
determination and dedication. They were fully cognizant of the powerful influences
which blocked the attainment of their goal. Yet they persisted in their efforts. And, as
almost always is the case, eventually they succeeded in winning approval.
So happy were these young men when told the good news that one of their number
wrote the stirring words for what has come down to us as "The Rho Owl Song." It is
a story in song of the stmggle that finally led to the founding of the Rho Chapter as
the last Chapter accepted and instaUed during the Nineteenth Century. The "Rampant
Lion" was the symbol of the Rho Kappa Upsilon Society. The "Owl," of course, repre
sents Psi UpsUon. Captured in song is the tale of how the "Rampant Lion" wooed and
won the "Ancient Owl," even though there were sinister forces abroad, endeavoring to
thwart this noble beast.
Much more could be gleaned from the Annals about the trials and tribulations of
other jewels in our diadem. All point to the virtues of courage, determination and
dedication. Would it not be a joy to behold for the alumni of the Rho and our other
inactive Chapters to re-arm themselves with the courage, determination and dedication
of their forebears? They must have inherited ff. AU they need is to show ff.

On August 20 and 21 all roads east, west, north
and south will lead to Syracuse, New York, where

decision-making, which will chart the course of the
Fraternity for the coming year. As always, the pro

affecting the future of Psi Upsilon.
Of especial significance is the governing process,
initiated at the first Convention of the Fraternity, and
held inviolate ever since. Two official undergraduate
delegates and one alumni delegate from each Chapter
may qualify to vote, according to the Constitution.
This insures that undergraduate members will have a
controlling majority in the consideration of all resolu
tions brought to the floor by one of the committees.
As is the case at every annual gathering of good

James B. Longley, Kappa '48, as was chronicled in
an earlier edition of The Diamond, has become one
of the celebrities of our
political world since his up
set victory last November over the two estabhshed
parties in the State of Maine. Brother Longley ran as
an independent and ran alone. His story adds further
lustre to the banners of Psi Upsilon.
The son of a streetcar conductor in Lewiston,
Maine, Brother Longley fits the model of the selfmade man. He is a fervent believer in the virtue of
hard work. To exemplify this he sleeps only about
three hours each night, jogs a mile every moming,
and does not conceal his ambition to do the best job
possible in anything he tackles.
As a youth Brother Longley worked in a textile mill
in order to support his widowed mother, his five sis
ters and brothers, and himself. He managed to make
his way to Bowdoin CoUege, did well there, and
turned to a career in insurance. That effort resulted
in the building of one of the largest insurance agen
cies in the State of Maine.
Long interested in politics, his decision to run for
the office of Governor in November, 1974 was trigThe Hon. James B. Longley

gered by two friends�John Gardner, of Common
Cause, and the late Lester Pearson, Prime Minister of
Canada. He was susceptible to their urging, having
become disillusioned by the ineffectiveness of the two
major parties. Once agreed, he infused into his cam
paign the same kind of zeal that he had demonstrated
in his business career. The result was his vrinning a
forty percent plurality of the votes cast in the elec
tion.

nomic woes of his native state could be remedied by
skUfful paring of the budget and by the attraction
of new business to Maine. He felt that a businesstype management could reduce the budget by at least

platforms of both major parties. Brother Longley re
minds his constituents that he actually is a registered
Democrat. Observers feel that he may have to shed
some of his independence if he is to secure the votes
necessary for the State legislature to pass his pro
grams. He remains confident, nevertheless, that what
he has proposed, and what he will propose, make the
kind of sense that should appeal to most legislators.
True to the commitment he has felt toward his
business career, he already has announced that he has
no intention of running for office a second time.
Some observers feel that he means what he says. Oth
ers believe that this is a ploy to attract support for his
programs in Augusta. Many are convinced that the
Governor already has proven that the "impossible
dream" can be attained and that he wiU succeed in ac
complishing the objectives for which the electorate
selected him.
As for the second term, this is one of those con
jectures which must remain speculative. It is not in
conceivable for the Democratic Party to adjust its
platform and endorse him for a second term.
Whatever else may be said about Brother Longley,
it is a fact that he awoke the day after election last
fall as a man acclaimed for achieving the impossible.
In succeeding months he has attracted no end of at
tention everywhere. And wherever he goes, he is an
example of a man who lives his beliefs and is proof
supreme that single-minded dedication to one's goal
can produce miracles.
